fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Blind Spot in Myth Theory", "body": "Lundwall took his doctorate at Pacifica Graduate Institute, the Joseph Campbell school of comparative myth, and says that eight years of coursework and dissertation writing left him staring at a lacuna: neither Campbell nor Jung, neither Harrison's myth and ritual school nor Eliade's sacred and profane, ever touched orality. He points to two books from the 1960s that reopened the question, Gerald Hawkins' Stonehenge Decoded and Giorgio de Santillana's Hamlet's Mill, both savaged on arrival. Richard Atkinson's rebuttal, titled Moonshine on Stonehenge, insisted the monument was built by howling barbarians. Hawkins, Lundwall notes, turned out to be right."}, {"title": "Camps That Followed the Sun", "body": "Rather than treat sky watching as a curiosity, Lundwall argues that oral peoples organized survival around it. He describes the Lakota, hunter gatherers who broke winter camp for spring camp and then summer camp not simply to chase herds but to follow the sun through their constellations, each camp representing a constellation so the ground carried a sky map while the sky carried a land map. Their original summer camp, he says, was Devils Tower in Wyoming. In the ancient Near East and in Egypt, he adds, you could not build a city until you had first built a temple and cosmicized the land."}, {"title": "How Knowledge Survived Without Writing", "body": "For ninety nine percent of human history there was no writing, so anything worth keeping had to be passed down in memorable form. Lundwall describes oral cultures telling the same knowledge in as many mediums as possible: oral narrative as myth, somatic narrative as dance, ritual timed to a rising sun, a heliacal star rising, or a phase of the moon. Every element in that web, the herd, the valley, the star, the season, gets personified, which is why he contends orality produces polytheism while monotheism is a product of literacy. Deity names, in his reading, work as technical terms, closer to verbs than nouns."}, {"title": "Analogy, Orion and the Rain Making Head", "body": "Oral peoples think analogically, Lundwall argues, and the Pyramid of Unas texts show it. Read glyph by glyph they sound like gibberish, telling you to open the sky door beside the baboon's penis, which one translator renders as the sword of Orion, sitting where the ecliptic crosses the Milky Way. They are not texts at all, he says, but ritual and cosmological scenarios that were danced, sung and chanted. The same logic, he contends, is why Maya and American Southwest cultures tied heads and scalps to rain ceremonies: a head arrives when a woman's water breaks, holds every divine function, and produces tears."}, {"title": "Cyclized History and the Flood as Rebirth", "body": "Because oral societies cannot keep footnoted histories, Lundwall says memory gets cyclized into archetypes of eternal return, and he answers Godfrey Higgins' Anacalypsis puzzle about the absence of history before Herodotus that way. His example is Caribbean vodou, where a village founder's spirit, recalled alongside the Loa, is gradually absorbed into the deity until the historical person is forgotten. He reads the biblical flood as the creation story retold beat for beat, and argues the flood that Utnapishtim recites in the Epic of Gilgamesh is not a clumsy insertion but a resurrection sequence, matching chapter 175 of the Papyrus of Ani."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Dr. John Knight Lundwall joins InnerVerse to discuss his groundbreaking book, Mythos and Cosmos: Mind and Meaning in the Oral Age. Picking up the torch where hundreds of years of academia missed the mark, Dr. Lundwall guides our understanding of mythology as a technical language akin to scientific jargon, exposes the epistemological wall between literacy and orality, explains the analogical aspect of oral myth via the example of human sacrifices, and ponders why oral cultures did not keep histories as we know them.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension we turn our discussion towards the category error of modernity to consider oral rites and stories as religion, question just what religion is through the example of the cult of state mandated "public health," the Renaissance prodigy Camillo and what his memory theater informs us of our own potential to recall complex ideas, the relationship between light pollution and literacy, and what it means to marry the best of both the oral and literary mind.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Religion as a Literate Category Error", "body": "Chance opens the extension by reading Lundwall's line that religion is a category of literacy, contrasting the literate hunger for orthodoxy with the oral pursuit of orthopraxy. Lundwall then lays out his problems with the word: no agreed definition across philosophy, theology and sociology departments, dictionary entries that define religion with the word itself, and no matching term in ancient Egyptian, Babylonian, Persian or Greek, nor among the indigenous peoples of Africa, the Americas or Aboriginal Australia. As he puts it, a people without the word probably lacked the concept, so for nearly all of history ritual simply reenacted what people observed."}, {"title": "Church, State and the Birth of a Word", "body": "Lundwall traces religion to a Latin term for binding oaths and ordinances performed for the cult of the state, arguing that for almost all of history church and state were one institution. That, he says, is where Dawkins, Harris and Dennett go wrong, blaming the priest who blessed a war while ignoring the magistrate who ordered it, and why Galileo's clerical critics were also the era's establishment academics. He then marks Christianity as the first world religion to begin with the management of texts, after Judaism, its First Temple cult destroyed, turned its temple into a text, with humanism only later splitting religion from the state."}, {"title": "The Supreme Good and Its Priesthood", "body": "Lundwall frames religion as a biological feature of consciousness: finite beings surrounded by infinite facts produce metaphysics, and the moment a culture settles on a supreme good, moral prescriptions, a teaching priesthood, rituals, hierarchy and punishments follow, whether it is monotheist, polytheist or atheist. Chance extends the model to the recent years, describing public health as a supreme good with mandated rituals and agencies acting as its priesthood, and ties health and morality together through Eusebius and the Therapeutae. Lundwall answers that abandoning the scientific method for political expediency never yields reason, since science's true opposite is politics."}, {"title": "Memory Theaters and Horizontal Knowledge", "body": "Chance reads the Phaedrus tale in which an Egyptian king warns that writing breeds forgetfulness, and asks about the Renaissance figure Camillo. Lundwall describes how Camillo turned a playhouse into a seven tiered model of the cosmos, one tier for each visible planet, and could recite whole fields of knowledge from its images. He adds Indian priests chanting the Vedas without error, and Walter Ong's account of a Siberian memory keeper who recited a poem heard once a year earlier. Oral minds excel at horizontal recall, he says, but only vertical, literate layering could ever build a microchip, while a Pueblo planting song doubled as a solar calendar."}, {"title": "Light Pollution and a Shrinking Cosmos", "body": "Chance shares his observation that rising literacy and digital technology track rising light pollution, hiding the sky he calls the original sacred text and internet. Lundwall recalls the 1994 Los Angeles earthquake blackout, when residents flooded fire departments and the Griffith Observatory with calls about a gas leak in the sky that was simply the Milky Way. He weighs the gains of electrification against an ontological loss, a universe now met through layered Hubble composites on computer screens. Asked whether the oral and literate minds can be married, he points to Utah's registered dark sky places and school sky programs, predicting we find the way after failing the wrong ones."}]
